The Bastard's recovery of the lion's hide and his killing of Austria (3.2) dramatize a son avenging his father and assuming his heroic identity — the swaggering 'Cordelion' spirit reborn in the play's most vital character. The lion-skin also carries an echo of Hercules's Nemean trophy, the classic emblem of borrowed valour.

cards.title: The Troublesome Raigne of King John

source.name: The Troublesome Raigne of John, King of England (anonymous, 1591)
source.citation: Anonymous two-part play The Troublesome Raigne of John, King of England (printed 1591), Shakespeare's principal dramatic source for King John.

cards.summary_basic: Shakespeare's King John is closely based on an earlier anonymous play, The Troublesome Raigne of King John (printed 1591). The older play supplied almost the entire plot — the inheritance scene, the Bastard Faulconbridge, the siege of Angiers, Arthur's death, the clash with Rome, and John's poisoning by a monk. Shakespeare tightens the structure, deepens the characters (above all Constance and the Bastard), and tones down the cruder anti-Catholic propaganda of his source.
cards.detail_scholar: The relationship is debated — most scholars hold that Shakespeare adapted the Troublesome Raigne (c. 1589–91), though a minority argue the older play is a memorial reconstruction derived from his. The Troublesome Raigne is stridently Protestant, staging lecherous friars and a lustful nun to mock the Church; Shakespeare keeps the anti-papal politics but drops the broad satire and makes John more morally ambiguous. He also adds the verbal grandeur the source lacks — Constance's laments and the Bastard's 'commodity' (self-interest) speech — turning a propaganda chronicle-play into a study of political expediency. It belongs with Holinshed, More, and the Famous Victories among the documented source-texts behind the histories.

cards.title: The King's Great Matter (Henry's divorce)

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Henry VIII's suit to annul his marriage to Katherine of Aragon — the legatine court at Blackfriars (1529) under Cardinals Wolsey and Campeius, and Katherine's appeal to Rome.

cards.summary_basic: The 'King's Great Matter' was Henry VIII's long campaign to annul his twenty-year marriage to Katherine of Aragon so that he could marry Anne Bullen. Henry claimed his conscience was troubled because Katherine had first been the wife of his dead elder brother Arthur, which (he argued from Leviticus) made their union unlawful. The play dramatizes the legatine trial at Blackfriars (2.4), where Katherine defends her marriage with unanswerable dignity, refuses to accept Wolsey as her judge, and appeals to the Pope before Campeius adjourns the case to Rome.
cards.detail_scholar: Katherine of Aragon, daughter of Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain, had married Henry's brother Prince Arthur, who died months later; she then wed Henry under a papal dispensation. Henry's later 'scruple' (Leviticus 18:16, 20:21, against marrying a brother's wife) was widely seen as a pretext for his desire for Anne and a male heir. Rome's refusal to grant the annulment — Katherine's nephew was the Emperor Charles V — led directly to the break with Rome. Drawing on Holinshed, Shakespeare and Fletcher make Katherine the clear moral victor of her trial while leaving Henry's true motives studiously ambiguous.

cards.title: The break with Rome and the English Reformation

source.name: Foxe, Acts and Monuments (1583); Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: John Foxe, Acts and Monuments (1583), and Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Henry VIII's repudiation of papal authority — the Act of Supremacy (1534) made the king Supreme Head of the Church of England, with Thomas Cranmer as Archbishop of Canterbury.

cards.summary_basic: When the Pope would not annul his marriage, Henry broke England's thousand-year obedience to Rome. By the Act of Supremacy (1534) he made himself Supreme Head of the Church of England, dissolved the monasteries, and had the reform-minded Archbishop Thomas Cranmer grant the divorce and crown Anne Bullen. The play touches this turning-point lightly but unmistakably: Cranmer's rise, and the hostility of the conservative Bishop Gardiner toward him in Act 5, reflect the religious struggle the divorce set loose.
cards.detail_scholar: Written under the Protestant-then-Stuart settlement, the play treats the Reformation with tact, since its consequences were still live. It celebrates Cranmer (later a Protestant martyr under Catholic Mary) and ends with the birth of Elizabeth, the Reformation's champion, but avoids open doctrinal polemic — unlike its source Foxe. Wolsey's fall and Cranmer's royal protection dramatize the shift of power from the old Cardinal-legate (Rome's man in England) to the new archbishop of the royal supremacy. King John's earlier defiance of the Pope was read by Tudor Protestants as a forerunner of this break.

cards.title: Cardinal Wolsey

source.name: George Cavendish, Life of Wolsey (c. 1557); Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: George Cavendish, The Life and Death of Cardinal Wolsey (written c. 1554–57), and Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on Thomas Wolsey (c. 1473–1530), Lord Chancellor and papal legate, and his fall in 1529–30.

cards.summary_basic: Thomas Wolsey, a butcher's son from Ipswich, rose to be Cardinal, Lord Chancellor, and papal legate — the most powerful man in England under Henry VIII, of almost royal magnificence (he built Hampton Court). The play traces his pride and fall: he destroys Buckingham, drives the divorce, and amasses huge wealth, until intercepted letters and an inventory of his riches expose his double-dealing. Stripped of office, he takes his celebrated farewell to 'all my greatness' and dies humbled (3.2).
cards.detail_scholar: Wolsey's failure to win the annulment from Rome ruined him: charged under praemunire (for asserting papal authority within the realm), he surrendered his goods, was arrested for treason, and died at Leicester Abbey in 1530 on his way to London. Shakespeare's sympathetic portrait of the fallen Cardinal — including the famous dying sentiment that had he served God as zealously as the king, God would not have left him 'naked to mine enemies' — draws on the intimate Life by his gentleman-usher George Cavendish. Griffith's even-handed obituary (4.2) credits Wolsey's vices and his virtues alike (he founded colleges at Oxford and Ipswich). His rise-and-fall is the play's central instance of the de casibus pattern.

cards.title: Foxe's Acts and Monuments (Book of Martyrs)

source.name: John Foxe, Acts and Monuments (1563; expanded 1583)
source.citation: John Foxe, Acts and Monuments of these Latter and Perilous Days (first English edition 1563; expanded 1583) — the great Protestant martyrology, a source for the Cranmer material in Henry VIII Act 5.

cards.summary_basic: Foxe's Acts and Monuments — popularly the 'Book of Martyrs' — was, after the Bible, the most influential book in Protestant England: a vast history of the Church told as the struggle of true believers against papal persecution. It supplied Henry VIII with its Act 5 material on Archbishop Cranmer — the plot of the conservative bishops to destroy him and his rescue by the king (the ring, the council scene) come from Foxe. Copies were chained in churches, and its martyr-stories shaped how the audience understood the Reformation.
cards.detail_scholar: Foxe celebrated Cranmer, burned under Catholic Mary in 1556, as a Protestant hero, and his account of the Henrician court furnished the dramatists with the 5.1–5.3 episode almost intact. The play's providential Protestant frame — climaxing in Cranmer's prophecy over the infant Elizabeth — is broadly Foxean, though Shakespeare and Fletcher mute the militant anti-Catholicism of their source. Foxe's authority helps explain why an English audience would readily accept Cranmer as the saintly counterweight to Bishop Gardiner.

cards.title: The Field of the Cloth of Gold

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587)
source.citation: Raphael Holinshed, Chronicles (1587), on the summit between Henry VIII and Francis I of France near Calais (the 'Field of the Cloth of Gold'), June 1520.

cards.summary_basic: The play opens with Norfolk's dazzled account of the Field of the Cloth of Gold — the spectacularly lavish summit of 1520 where Henry VIII and the young French king Francis I met near Calais in a fortnight-long contest of magnificence, with cloth-of-gold tents, tournaments, and feasting (1.1). Buckingham observes that Cardinal Wolsey stage-managed the whole ruinous extravagance, and that the peace it celebrated was already crumbling — introducing both Wolsey's overweening power and the play's theme of dazzling pomp over substance.
cards.detail_scholar: The 1520 meeting near Guisnes and Ardres (the play's 'Guynes and Arde') cost both crowns enormous sums and sealed an Anglo-French amity that collapsed within two years when Henry allied instead with the Emperor Charles V. Shakespeare uses Norfolk's set-piece description to establish a world of costly ceremony and to plant the nobles' resentment of the low-born Cardinal who 'order'd' such grandeur, as Buckingham complains, largely 'without the privity o' the king.' The episode sets the play's recurring contrast between glittering show and the hard realities of power.

cards.title: Cranmer's prophecy over the infant Elizabeth

source.name: Holinshed, Chronicles (1587); the play's own invention
source.citation: Henry VIII 5.5; the christening of Princess Elizabeth (later Elizabeth I), 10 September 1533. The prophecy is the dramatists' invention, written in hindsight from the reigns of Elizabeth (d. 1603) and James I.

cards.summary_basic: The play climaxes with the christening of the infant Elizabeth, over whom Archbishop Cranmer delivers a prophecy (5.5): the child will be a 'pattern to all princes,' bringing an age of peace and plenty, and like a phoenix her greatness will pass undimmed to a successor. For Shakespeare's audience this was history foretold — Elizabeth I had been their long-reigned queen, and the promised 'heir' is a flattering nod to the reigning James I. The scene turns a court chronicle into a celebration of the Tudor–Stuart providential destiny.
cards.detail_scholar: The prophecy is panegyric written with hindsight — the play dates to 1613, a decade into James's reign. Cranmer promises that Elizabeth shall be 'a pattern to all princes,' a 'maiden phoenix' from whose ashes a new heir (James) shall rise 'as great in admiration as herself.' It weaves in biblical images of peace — every man safe 'under his own vine what he plants' (echoing Micah 4:4 and 1 Kings 4:25) — and the wisdom of the Queen of Sheba ('Saba'). Retroactively it frames the whole turbulent reign of Henry VIII as the providential prelude to England's golden age, aligning the play with the larger Tudor myth.

cards.title: The Bermuda wreck of the Sea Venture (1609)

source.name: Strachey, A True Reportory (1610); Jourdain, Discovery of the Barmudas (1610)
source.citation: William Strachey, 'A True Reportory of the Wracke and Redemption of Sir Thomas Gates, Knight' (letter dated 15 July 1610; printed 1625 in Purchas His Pilgrimes); Sylvester Jourdain, 'A Discovery of the Barmudas' (1610). The Sea Venture wrecked on Bermuda in a hurricane, July 1609. Cf. The Tempest 1.2, 'the still-vex'd Bermoothes.'

cards.summary_basic: In 1609 the Sea Venture, flagship of a fleet bound for the Virginia colony, was driven by a hurricane onto the reefs of Bermuda; all aboard survived, wintered on the supposedly devil-haunted island, built two new ships, and reached Jamestown in 1610. Eyewitness accounts — chiefly William Strachey's letter — reached London just as Shakespeare wrote The Tempest, and are its most-cited topical source: the tempest, the 'still-vex'd Bermoothes,' the fire on the rigging, and the miraculously unharmed castaways all echo the reports.
cards.detail_scholar: Strachey's 'True Reportory' (written 1610, not printed until 1625, so Shakespeare likely read it in manuscript) describes a storm of exactly the play's kind, the eerie fire Ariel evokes when he 'flam'd amazement' on the rigging (St Elmo's fire), the abundance of the uninhabited island, and quarrels and a mutiny among the stranded men — analogues to the Stephano-Caliban plot. Bermuda was reputed an 'Ile of Divels.' Shakespeare moves his island to the Mediterranean, but Ariel's errand to fetch dew 'from the still-vex'd Bermoothes' (1.2) winks at the source. The episode also ties the play to the Virginia Company's colonial enterprise, the backdrop to its nature-and-empire themes.

cards.title: Montaigne, 'Of the Cannibals'

source.name: Montaigne, Essais (Florio's translation, 1603)
source.citation: Michel de Montaigne, 'Of the Cannibals' (Des Cannibales, Essais I.31), in John Florio's English translation, 1603. Gonzalo's ideal-commonwealth speech, The Tempest 2.1.148-169, paraphrases it directly.

cards.summary_basic: Montaigne's essay 'Of the Cannibals' (c. 1580; Englished by John Florio in 1603) argues that the 'savage' peoples of the New World live closer to virtuous nature than civilized Europeans, who are the real barbarians. Shakespeare knew Florio's version: Gonzalo's daydream of an ideal commonwealth with 'no kind of traffic... no name of magistrate... no occupation' (2.1) lifts a whole passage almost word for word, and the essay feeds the play's debate over nature, culture, and who is truly 'civil.'
cards.detail_scholar: Florio's Montaigne describes a nation that has 'no kinde of traffike, no knowledge of letters, no intelligence of numbers, no name of magistrate, nor of politike superioritie' — Gonzalo's speech follows it clause by clause, then is mocked by Antonio and Sebastian ('The latter end of his commonwealth forgets the beginning'). The essay's larger claim — that European 'civility' may be more barbarous than the cannibals' simplicity — runs through the Prospero-Caliban relationship and the play's questioning of nature versus nurture. The name 'Caliban' is widely read as an anagram or near-echo of 'cannibal' (itself from 'Carib'). Montaigne is one of the play's two firmest topical sources, alongside the Bermuda narratives.

cards.title: Setebos, Caliban's god

source.name: Pigafetta's Magellan voyage, in Eden's History of Travel (1577)
source.citation: Antonio Pigafetta's account of Magellan's 1520 voyage, Englished in Richard Eden, 'The History of Travayle in the West and East Indies' (1577): the Patagonian 'giants' invoke a great devil, 'Setebos.' Caliban swears by 'Setebos, my dam's god' (The Tempest 1.2; cf. 5.1).

cards.summary_basic: Setebos was a god — reported as a 'great devil' — of the Patagonians of South America, recorded by a survivor of Magellan's circumnavigation and printed in English in Richard Eden's 1577 collection of travel narratives. Shakespeare borrowed the exotic name for the deity of Caliban's witch-mother Sycorax: Caliban fears Prospero's art 'would control my dam's god, Setebos' (1.2), and at the end marvels, 'O Setebos, these be brave spirits indeed!' (5.1).
cards.detail_scholar: The name comes from one of the era's most widely read travel books: Eden's translation of Pigafetta's report that the towering 'giants' of Patagonia, when seized, roared upon their god Setebos. Its appearance in The Tempest is a small but telling sign of how the play absorbs New World voyage literature: Caliban's religion is given a real, documented 'savage' deity, locating Sycorax's witchcraft in the same ethnographic imagination as the Bermuda and Montaigne material. It is among the clearest verbal borrowings from the travel narratives in the play.

cards.title: John Gower and the Confessio Amantis

source.name: John Gower, Confessio Amantis (c. 1390)
source.citation: John Gower, Confessio Amantis (c. 1390), Book 8 — the tale of Apollonius of Tyre, the main source of Pericles. The poet appears 'as Chorus' and narrates the play.

cards.summary_basic: John Gower (c. 1330-1408) was a major English poet, a friend of Chaucer, whose long poem Confessio Amantis ('The Lover's Confession') retells the ancient romance of Apollonius of Tyre — the story Pericles dramatizes. Shakespeare brings the poet himself onstage as the Presenter, 'ancient Gower... from ashes,' who speaks an old-fashioned rhymed chorus before every act, introduces the silent dumb-shows, and points the moral at the close.
cards.detail_scholar: Using Gower as Chorus is a deliberate antiquarian effect: his pointedly archaic four-beat couplets ('To sing a song that old was sung, / From ashes ancient Gower is come') signal that the audience is hearing a venerable medieval tale, one 'sung at festivals, / On ember-eves and holy-ales.' Gower bridges the play's huge leaps of time and place ('I do beseech you / To learn of me, who stand i' the gaps to teach you'), turning the episodic, decades-spanning romance into a narrated story-within-a-frame and using dumb-shows to compress action he then glosses 'with speech.' The device shaped both the play's old reputation as a 'mouldy tale' and its modern revival as a sophisticated experiment in storytelling.

cards.title: The romance of Apollonius of Tyre

source.name: Historia Apollonii regis Tyri; Twine, The Patterne of Painefull Adventures (1576)
source.citation: The anonymous Latin romance 'Historia Apollonii regis Tyri' (c. 5th-6th century AD); Englished by Laurence Twine as 'The Patterne of Painefull Adventures' (c. 1576, reprinted 1607), Shakespeare's source alongside Gower's Confessio Amantis.

cards.summary_basic: Behind Pericles lies one of the most popular stories of the Middle Ages: the Latin romance of Apollonius of Tyre — a prince driven by shipwreck and fortune across the Mediterranean, parted from his wife and daughter and reunited with them years later. Shakespeare follows it through two English versions, Gower's poem and Laurence Twine's prose 'Patterne of Painefull Adventures,' changing the hero's name from Apollonius to Pericles.
cards.detail_scholar: The 'Historia Apollonii regis Tyri' survives in dozens of medieval manuscripts and languages; its episodic shape — a riddle of incest, storms, apparent deaths, a daughter preserved in a brothel by her virtue, and a recognition scene and temple reunion — is the skeleton of Pericles. Twine's prose redaction (entered 1576, reprinted 1607, just as the play was written) supplied much narrative detail, while Gower's verse supplied the frame. Shakespeare's renaming of Apollonius as 'Pericles' may glance at the noble Pyrocles of Sidney's Arcadia. The play's collaborative text (likely Shakespeare with George Wilkins, who also issued a 1608 prose 'Painfull Adventures of Pericles') reflects this layered descent.
